body.text: Former students of Our Lady of Dolours Catholic school take legal action over alleged historical abuse
In short:
Three former students allege they were assaulted by parish priest Father Paul Francis Cahill at Our Lady of Dolours Catholic Church in Chatswood in the 1970s and 1980s.
A retired priest said he witnessed Father Cahill, now deceased, sexually abuse a young boy and he reported it to the church.
Infamous triple-murderer Sef Gonzales was an altar boy at the same parish, and in a recent appeal of his life sentence, said he was abused by a priest as a child.
Three former students of a Sydney Catholic school are suing the church, alleging they were sexually assaulted as children by a priest.

One alleged victim described Father Paul Francis Cahill as a "sneaky and manipulative" man who "ingratiated himself" with families in the parish to gain their trust, and therefore greater access to their sons.
The three men are taking their claims to the NSW Supreme Court. They allege that they were abused between the late 1970s and the 1980s while attending Our Lady of Dolours Primary School in Chatswood.
Their accounts are supported by a retired priest who said he witnessed and reported the sexual abuse of a fourth child to the church, but no action was taken.
One former student, Christopher*, alleged the now-deceased priest sexually abused him on two separate occasions in the early 1980s during school hours.

"I was sexually abused by a Catholic priest who was the head of the parish, having been sent across to the presbytery from my primary school, which sits adjacent to the church," Christopher told the ABC.
He said he was told to attend the presbytery to prepare for church readings.
Christopher has commenced legal action against the Archdiocese of Sydney as well as Catholic Schools NSW for damages caused by child sexual abuse.
Two other alleged victims, David* and Thomas*, are also taking action against the church, with all three claiming Father Cahill sexually assaulted them as boys.
Christopher told the ABC he holds the church and school responsible for allowing him to be alone with Father Cahill, who died in 2017.
"My belief is that the church was aware of the abuse and that I was not the first victim,"
he said.

"I'm also of the belief that the primary school leadership was culpable for sending a young boy, alone, to be in the company of a priest — regardless of awareness of previous indiscretions or complaints."
Christopher said he did not report the abuse and repressed the memories for most of his life, only recalling the events two years ago.
The second litigant, David*, alleged he was abused "weekly" as an altar boy in the mid-to-late 1980's, and estimates between 50 and 100 instances of abuse.
"I was systematically and repeatedly sexually abused as an eight-to-10-year-old by a priest," David said.
"The abuse was perpetrated by Father Paul Cahill in multiple areas across the church, sacristy, and presbytery."
David told the ABC he also believed the church knew of concerns about Father Cahill and is now seeking acknowledgement and compensation.

"[It has had] a devastating impact in all forms of life, in every way imaginable. Broken marriage, lifelong financial hardship, ingrained trust issues, public humiliation and shame. The list goes on and on."
David said he did not report the abuse at the time and only began telling others seven years ago.
The third litigant, Thomas*, said he was abused by Father Cahill in the late 1970s and 1980s, and reported this to the church, but nothing was done.
The ABC understands the church conducted its own investigation into Thomas's claims.
Our Lady of Dolours Church was originally part of the Archdiocese of Sydney but became part of the new Diocese of Broken Bay when it was created by late Pope John Paul II in 1986.
A spokesperson for the Diocese of Broken Bay declined an interview.
"As these matters are the subject of ongoing legal proceedings, it would not be appropriate to comment further," the spokesperson said.
"The Diocese of Broken Bay takes seriously concerns raised and encourages anyone with information or concerns to contact New South Wales police or the Diocese of Broken Bay's Safeguarding Office.
"The Diocese of Broken Bay is deeply committed to Safeguarding and acknowledges the profound and lasting harm caused by any abuse, and the courage of those who come forward."
Abuse reported to church, retired priest says
A retired catholic priest, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, told the ABC that he witnessed Father Cahill sexually assault a fourth boy.
"I observed Father Paul Cahill abusing a person younger than 16 years, during the early 1990s," he said.
The priest said he reported the incident to the church at the "earliest opportunity".
Father Cahill continued to work at the parish, but was later moved to the nearby parish of Killara, where his contact with children was greatly reduced.
The diocese spokesperson did not address questions about the alleged report by the retired priest or other warnings about his conduct, citing the legal action.

"The safety of children and vulnerable people is a priority of the diocese, and anyone with information or concerns is encouraged to contact NSW Police or the Diocese's Safeguarding Office," the spokesperson said.
The Archdiocese of Sydney did not respond to requests for comment and Catholic Schools NSW declined to comment.
All three former students are represented by Maurice Blackburn.

"Maurice Blackburn acts for a number of survivors who allege they were abused by the same priest while attending Our Lady of Dolours Catholic School and Church in the 1980s," lead solicitor Jacqueline Grace said.
"They want the church to be held accountable for what happened to them as children. They want justice for the harm caused that remains with them every single day."
Priest visited 'baby-faced killer' in prison
Father Cahill made headlines in 2004 as an advocate for triple murderer Sef Gonzales, who had brutally murdered his parents and sister three years earlier.
Gonzales and his family were parishioners of Our Lady of Dolours church, and a young Gonzales served as an altar boy.
Even after his conviction was handed down, Gonzales, also known as the "baby-faced killer", retained the support of Father Cahill, who proclaimed his innocence from the pulpit.
The priest continued to visit him weekly in prison, maintaining he believed Gonzales.
Last year, Gonzales won the right to appeal his life sentence after evidence of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) emerged.
The murderer argued he had been in denial about PTSD symptoms as a result of being sexually assaulted by a priest as a child.
A directions hearing on his sentence appeal is listed for next month.
Gonzales has already appealed his conviction on these grounds, but his appeal was dismissed.
Gonzales has not said who allegedly abused him, only that the abuse began shortly after he arrived in Sydney from the Philippines as a 10-year-old.
Gonzales has a history of dishonesty, and falsely claimed his family were murdered in a hate crime. In 2004, he was found guilty of their murders and is serving three concurrent life sentences.
*Names changed for legal and privacy reasons.
